props.name: any H2:CO ratio; best about 4:1; not below stoichiometric, not above 6:1

evidence.quote: My catalyst will form methanol from a gas mixture having any ratio of hydrogen to carbon monoxide, but
if the ratio is below one to one by volume the 8. T. Y. will be considerably lower than that obtained with hydrogen in excess by volume.
I have found that a gas containing about four volumes of hydrogen to each volume of carbon monoxide gives the best results, and that with about 6 volumes of hydrogen the S. T. Y. is somewhat lower.
For eco- nomic reasons I therefore prefer not to ex- ceed 6 volumes of hydrogen for each vol- ume of carbon monoxide,

props.statement: The catalyst forms methanol from any H2:CO ratio, but below 1:1 by volume the space time yield is considerably lower; less hydrogen than the stoichiometric 2H2+CO=CH3OH is not preferred; about 4 volumes H2 per volume CO gives the best results, about 6 volumes a somewhat lower S.T.Y., and 6 is preferably not exceeded for economic reasons.

props.name: unsupported catalyst advantageously pilled before reduction

evidence.quote: I have also found it ad- vantageous, when no support is used, to-
compress powdered catalysts into the form of pills. This pill formation is preferably carried out with the unreduced_ precipitate after which the pills are subjected to the reducing action.
I have found that pills about one-fourth inch in diameter and one- eighth inch thick give good results.

props.statement: When no support is used it is advantageous to compress the powdered catalyst into pills, preferably from the unreduced precipitate, which are then reduced; pills about 1/4 inch in diameter and 1/8 inch thick give good results.

props.name: methanol from 5 atm up (even 1 atm below 200 °C); preferred 50-400 atm

evidence.quote: formed in substantial amounts by these cat- alysts at pressures of ‘five atmospheres and upwards dependent on the temperature used.
Substantial yields’ of methanol may even be obtained at pressures lower than five atmospheres, for example, one atmos- phere by operating at temperatures below 200° C.
the S. T. Y. is in general so much lower that the process would not be economical. In general I prefer to operate at pressures be- tween about 50 and 400 atmospheres.

props.statement: Within 150-400 °C methanol is formed in substantial amounts at five atmospheres and upwards depending on temperature; substantial yields may even be obtained below five atmospheres, e.g. one atmosphere below 200 °C, but the S.T.Y. is then uneconomically low; pressures of about 50-400 atmospheres are preferred.

props.name: reduction: hydrogen, CO or methanol; dilute with inert gas

evidence.quote: Lhe reduction can be carried out by any suitable means, such as passing hydrogen, or mixtures of hydrogen with carbon mon- oxide or methanol or both over the heated
In order to prevent large, uncontroll-_ able increases in temperature during reduc- tion it is usually desirable to dilute the re- ducing gas with nitrogen or any other inert gas.
Hor example, a satisfactory reducing mixture is 5 volumes of methyl alcohol vapor, and 95 volumes of nitrogen.
This reducing mixture is passed at atmospheric pressure over the dried precipitate prefer- auly contained in a copper lined vessel and heated to not over 350° C. and preferably to about 150-200° C.

props.statement: The reduction may use hydrogen or mixtures of hydrogen with carbon monoxide or methanol; to prevent large uncontrollable temperature rises the reducing gas is usually diluted with nitrogen or another inert gas, e.g. 5 volumes methanol vapour and 95 volumes nitrogen at atmospheric pressure, heating to not over 350 °C and preferably about 150-200 °C.

props.name: higher S.V.H. raises S.T.Y., lowers conversion

props.statement: If the space velocity is increased, the space time yield increases and the percent conversion of CO to methanol decreases.
